texts.title: Urban orchards
texts.text: In the early 2010s, the small city of Marlow had almost no fruit trees within its boundaries. Then a group of residents began planting apple, pear and plum trees on unused patches of land, with the permission of the city council. Within six years, the project had grown to forty-two sites and was supported by around three hundred volunteers. Fruit picked from the trees is shared freely, and any surplus is made into juice that is sold at a weekly market. The money raised pays for new trees and tools. Not everyone welcomed the idea at first: some neighbours worried that fallen fruit would attract wasps and make pavements slippery. The organisers responded by arranging regular collection days. A recent survey found that people living near an orchard were more likely to know their neighbours' names than those living elsewhere in the city. Organisers now hope to teach pruning skills in local schools, although no date has been fixed.

paragraphs.A: When the Harbor Bay Reading Room opened in 1894, it consisted of a single shelf of donated books kept at the back of a fish market. Membership cost one penny a week.
paragraphs.B: By 1920 the collection had outgrown the market, and the town raised funds for a purpose-built hall. Much of the money came from a travelling theatre that donated a season of ticket sales.
paragraphs.C: During the 1980s, falling budgets forced the library to close on three days each week. Local volunteers stepped in to keep the doors open, running story sessions for children and helping elderly readers choose books.
paragraphs.D: Today the library lends not only books but also tools, musical instruments and seeds. Staff say this reflects a broader view of what a community can share.

sections.directions: Listen and complete the form. Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER, then answer the multiple-choice questions.

audio_text.text: Receptionist: Good morning, Greenfield Community Centre.
Caller: Hello, I would like to register for the pottery workshop.
Receptionist: Certainly. Could I have your surname?
Caller: Oh seven seven double zero, nine four five, three one two.
Receptionist: The workshop runs on Wednesday evenings at half past six.
Receptionist: Forty-five pounds for six sessions, and clay is included.
Receptionist: Yes, behind the building, but only after five o'clock.
Tutor: So, Daniel, how is your project on coastal erosion going?
Daniel: I have collected most of the data, but I am not sure whether to focus on one beach or compare two.
Tutor: With only six weeks left, I would advise one beach, and do it properly.
Daniel: That makes sense. Then I could spend extra time on the interviews with local fishermen.
Tutor: Good idea. And send me your draft by the end of the month.

choices.text: When to hand in the project
Whether to study one beach or two
Compare as many beaches as possible

items.stem: When should Daniel send his draft?

choices.text: By the end of the month

tasks.prompt: The table shows the percentage of households with internet access in the fictional region of Eastvale in three different years. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
A neighbour has been playing loud music late at night. Write a letter to the neighbour. In your letter, explain the problem, say how it affects you, and suggest what could be done.
Some people think that children should learn a foreign language from the age of six. Others think it is better to start later. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Many cities now offer free public transport. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
In some countries, people work from home several days a week. What are the benefits and drawbacks of this trend for employees and for employers?
Museums should be free for everyone. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
